transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I came in today because... it's actually been really embarrassing lately, especially at work. I'm a jeweler, you see, mostly working with precious stones and metal, lots of custom settings and repairs. I've been doing it a long time, so I know my way around a bench and I'm usually very good with the customers. 

But lately, when people ask me a really simple question, I just... I can't seem to give them a simple answer. Like, just the other day, a customer asked me when her ring repair would be ready. It was a simple sizing job, so all I needed to say was Thursday afternoon. But instead, my answer just started going all over the place. I opened my mouth and started talking about the invoices we use, because the blue slips were sitting right there on the counter, and then that somehow reminded me of the garden soil I bought over the weekend because the bags were heavy and I had to sign a receipt for them, and before I knew it, I was rambling on to this poor woman about my mortgage papers and the bank. 

And I could just see her face changing. I could see her losing me, you know? The customers just look at me like they have no idea how we got from a broken ring to garden soil. It's like my brain just won't stay on a straight track anymore, and I just keep stringing all these completely unrelated things together, and I know I'm doing it while it's happening but I can't seem to reel it back in.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed your mood being unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable, along with feeling like you have much more energy than usual?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Elevated? Definitely not. If anything, it's the exact opposite, you know? I haven't felt euphoric in... well, I can't even remember the last time I felt anything close to that. And as for energy, I'm just so tired. I mean, I drag myself out of bed, I get to the shop, I turn the lights on, I unlock the cases, and by the time I've even set up my bench for the day, I feel like I've run a marathon. 

There's no extra energy, no feeling like I can take on the world or anything like that. I used to have days where I'd stay late at the shop, working on a custom piece, just really getting into the flow of setting the stones, feeling really good about it. But lately, I just watch the clock, waiting until I can lock up and go home and just sit. I don't feel irritable in a... in an energetic way, either. I mean, I get frustrated with myself when I start rambling to the customers, like I told you about, but that's just because I'm embarrassed, not because I'm keyed up or anything. So, no, definitely no high moods or extra energy. Just... just feeling very drained, honestly.
Have you experienced anything like hearing voices or seeing things that others don't, or having thoughts or beliefs that others have told you seem unusual or not true?

Well, um... yes, actually. It's... it's strange, and I haven't really wanted to tell anyone about it because it sounds so odd, you know? But since you're asking... well, it happens mostly when I'm at the shop. My shop is usually pretty quiet, especially in the early mornings before we open or late in the afternoon if it's a slow day, which we've had a lot of lately. And when it gets really quiet like that, just the hum of the refrigerator in the breakroom or the ticking of the wall clock... I'll be sitting at my bench, maybe sorting some loose stones or inspecting a clasp, and I'll hear this voice. 

It's a woman's voice. And she just... she mutters my name. Just my name, but it sounds like it's coming from the polishing room in the back. The first few times it happened, I actually got up and walked all the way back there, thinking maybe one of the girls from the front had come back to ask me something, or maybe a customer had wandered past the counter, which they really aren't supposed to do, but it happens. But every time I check, the room is completely empty. The buffer isn't running, the lights are half-dimmed, and there's absolutely no one there. But the voice sounds so real, Dr. Smith. It's not like a thought in my head, it's like someone is standing just a few feet away, just out of sight, whispering to me. 

And then there's the smell. That's the other thing. You see, when you work with metal—gold, silver, platinum—you use a jeweler's torch. It's a very specific smell when the metal gets hot, almost sharp and metallic, like burning ozone and hot flux. I know that smell better than I know my own perfume. But lately, I've been smelling it when all the torches are completely off. The tanks are closed, the valves are shut, the bench is cold. But I'll just be sitting there, and suddenly this overwhelming smell of burning metal just fills my nose. It's so strong that I actually stop what I'm doing and go check all the stations, checking the lines, checking the regulators, terrified that there's a leak or something is smoldering. But it's always fine. Nothing is burning. But I smell it so clearly, just like I hear that woman's voice. It's really starting to unnerve me, to be honest, because I know I'm the only one there, but my senses are telling me something completely different.

Thinking back, did the depressive symptoms—the exhaustion and low mood—start before, after, or around the same time as when you first began hearing the voice and smelling the burning metal, and have there been any periods where you heard or smelled these things while your mood and energy were completely normal?

Well, if I really think back on it... it’s a little fuzzy because the days kind of blend together when you’re just sitting at the bench for hours on end, but... actually, the strange things started before I got so incredibly drained. Yes, definitely before. 

Because I remember there was this stretch of time—this was before the depression really settled in and made everything feel so terribly heavy—where I was actually feeling quite like myself. My energy was completely normal. I was still running my evening classes at the shop. I teach a beginner's jewelry-making class, mostly just basic wire-wrapping and simple bezel settings, you know, nothing too complex, but it still takes a lot of stamina to hover over six different students and make sure no one burns themselves. And I was still gardening on the weekends, too. That’s why I had bought all that heavy garden soil I mentioned earlier, I was out there on my hands and knees getting the flowerbeds completely overhauled for the season, and I felt perfectly fine doing it. 

But even then, during that really active stretch when my mood was perfectly fine, I was having those strange experiences. For several weeks, I just kept hearing noises coming from the polishing room. The polishing room is all the way in the back of the shop, past the employee breakroom, and it's usually closed off because of the dust, but I would just constantly hear things back there while I was teaching or working. And on top of that, I started getting so terribly worried that the customers were watching the business. 

I don't mean just window shopping, which is what you want them to do, obviously. I mean, I was convinced they were standing out on the sidewalk, just staring in, watching the shop, watching me work. I'd be showing a student how to use the jeweler's saw or planting my hydrangeas at home, feeling completely energetic and normal, but I'd have this overwhelming worry that people were keeping tabs on the business, just waiting out there. It was so unsettling. So, yes, to answer your question, those things—the noises in the back, the worrying about being watched—that all went on for several weeks while my mood and my energy were still completely normal, long before I started feeling so tired and low.

Do you have any medical conditions—like a neurological problem, head injury, or recent illness—or are you taking any medications, or using alcohol or recreational drugs, that could be linked to when the voices and smells started?

No, no, nothing like that at all. I mean, my health has actually always been surprisingly good, which is a blessing considering how much time I spend hunched over a jeweler's bench. I haven't had any head injuries... well, I mean, I bumped my head on an open cabinet door in the breakroom maybe three years ago, but it didn't even leave a bruise, it just startled me more than anything. And definitely no neurological problems or recent illnesses. I actually just had my annual physical with my primary care doctor—he's been seeing me for, oh, gosh, it has to be fifteen years now—and he said my blood pressure was fantastic, my cholesterol was right where it should be, and there was absolutely nothing wrong with me physically. I haven't even had a cold this past winter, which is honestly a miracle because my evening students are always coming in with the sniffles and coughing all over the tools.

As for medications, I don't take anything. Not even a daily vitamin, though my sister keeps telling me I need to start taking calcium now that I'm in my fifties, but I just try to get it from my diet, you know, yogurt and things like that. Sometimes I'll take an ibuprofen if my hands ache from gripping the pliers too long when I'm doing wire-wrapping, but that's really it. 

And alcohol or recreational drugs... oh, absolutely not. I mean, I'll have half a glass of champagne at a wedding, maybe, or a sip of wine at a holiday dinner, but I don't really like the taste of alcohol, and it always just makes me feel sleepy anyway. Plus, when you work with precious stones and hot torches all day, you need a completely steady hand and a crystal clear head. You just can't be doing that sort of delicate work if you're drinking or taking anything. One slip of the graver and you've ruined a two-thousand-dollar sapphire, or you've burned your own finger on the soldering block. So, no, definitely no drugs, no drinking, no medications, and no physical illnesses that I know of. I know I've been feeling terribly exhausted lately, but physically speaking, my body is perfectly healthy. There's just... there's no outside reason for why I'd be hearing or smelling those things.

In total, how many weeks or months has it been since the voices and burning smell first started until now, and how much of that entire time have you also been feeling this level of depressed and exhausted?

Well, goodness, trying to pin down exactly how many weeks or months it’s been on the calendar is... well, it’s difficult, because when you feel like this, time just sort of stretches out and loses all its meaning. The days just bleed into one another when you're sitting at the jeweler's bench for hours on end. But if I really sit and look at the whole picture, from that very first time I heard the whispering and smelled the burning metal, up until right now... well, for most of the time this has been going on, that heavy, bleak mood has been right there overshadowing everything. 

It’s not just been a few brief bad weeks here and there, you know, like when you just have a slump because business is slow or the weather is dreary. No, it’s been the vast majority of the time. For most of this whole ordeal, the poor sleep, the completely low appetite, the guilt... they've all just become a regular part of my daily life. 

I mean, the sleep is just dreadful—I'll lie awake for hours just staring at the ceiling, thinking about all the unfinished repairs sitting in my safe, and then by the time morning actually comes, I'm already bone-tired. And my appetite is just completely gone. I used to love walking down to the little deli on the corner from the shop to get a nice turkey sandwich or a salad for my lunch break, but lately, I can barely force down a few plain crackers at my desk. And then there's the guilt... oh, the guilt is just constant. I feel terrible that I'm not giving my evening students the lively, energetic teacher they paid for, and I feel guilty that I can't just snap out of this funk and run my business the way I used to. 

So, yes, while there was that stretch at the very beginning where my energy was fine, if you look at the entire time this has been happening, for most of it, the bleak mood and all these other awful feelings have been an everyday reality for me. It really hasn't just been a passing phase at all.

As for medications, I don't take anything. Not even a daily vitamin, though my sister keeps telling me I need to start taking calcium now that I'm in my fifties, but I just try to get it from my diet, you know, yogurt and things like that. Sometimes I'll take an ibuprofen if my hands ache from gripping the pliers too long when I'm doing wire-wrapping, but that's really it. 

And alcohol or recreational drugs... oh, absolutely not. I mean, I'll have half a glass of champagne at a wedding, maybe, or a sip of wine at a holiday dinner, but I don't really like the taste of alcohol, and it always just makes me feel sleepy anyway. Plus, when you work with precious stones and hot torches all day, you need a completely steady hand and a crystal clear head. You just can't be doing that sort of delicate work if you're drinking or taking anything. One slip of the graver and you've ruined a two-thousand-dollar sapphire, or you've burned your own finger on the soldering block. So, no, definitely no drugs, no drinking, no medications, and no physical illnesses that I know of. I know I've been feeling terribly exhausted lately, but physically speaking, my body is perfectly healthy. There's just... there's no outside reason for why I'd be hearing or smelling those things.

inference.note: Medical workup (physical exam, labs) is unremarkable and there is no medication, substance, or neurological cause identified, making an organic/secondary psychotic disorder (F06.2) unlikely and it has been removed. The psychotic symptoms (auditory and olfactory hallucinations, persecutory delusions) clearly preceded the mood/energy changes by several weeks while functioning was normal, supporting a primary psychotic disorder; whether the depressive episode is concurrent enough to meet schizoaffective criteria versus representing a post-psychotic depressive episode in schizophrenia remains to be clarified.

doctor.intent: Determine the overall duration of continuous illness (psychotic symptoms) and whether the depressive episode has lasted for a substantial portion of that total illness duration, to distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder
doctor.question: In total, how many weeks or months has it been since the voices and burning smell first started until now, and how much of that entire time have you also been feeling this level of depressed and exhausted?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: For most of the time this has been going on, the bleak mood, poor sleep, low appetite, and guilt have been part of my daily life, not just brief bad weeks.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the total duration of the psychotic symptoms and what proportion of that entire time the depressive symptoms have been present, which directly assesses whether the mood episode has been present for the majority of the illness duration (Criterion C).

patient.answer:
Well, goodness, trying to pin down exactly how many weeks or months it’s been on the calendar is... well, it’s difficult, because when you feel like this, time just sort of stretches out and loses all its meaning. The days just bleed into one another when you're sitting at the jeweler's bench for hours on end. But if I really sit and look at the whole picture, from that very first time I heard the whispering and smelled the burning metal, up until right now... well, for most of the time this has been going on, that heavy, bleak mood has been right there overshadowing everything. 

It’s not just been a few brief bad weeks here and there, you know, like when you just have a slump because business is slow or the weather is dreary. No, it’s been the vast majority of the time. For most of this whole ordeal, the poor sleep, the completely low appetite, the guilt... they've all just become a regular part of my daily life. 

I mean, the sleep is just dreadful—I'll lie awake for hours just staring at the ceiling, thinking about all the unfinished repairs sitting in my safe, and then by the time morning actually comes, I'm already bone-tired. And my appetite is just completely gone. I used to love walking down to the little deli on the corner from the shop to get a nice turkey sandwich or a salad for my lunch break, but lately, I can barely force down a few plain crackers at my desk. And then there's the guilt... oh, the guilt is just constant. I feel terrible that I'm not giving my evening students the lively, energetic teacher they paid for, and I feel guilty that I can't just snap out of this funk and run my business the way I used to. 

So, yes, while there was that stretch at the very beginning where my energy was fine, if you look at the entire time this has been happening, for most of it, the bleak mood and all these other awful feelings have been an everyday reality for me. It really hasn't just been a passing phase at all.

inference.note: The patient reports several weeks of psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations, olfactory hallucinations, delusions of being watched) occurring while mood and energy were completely normal, which rules against pure F20.0 given the mood episode duration is substantial but not the entirety of the illness. However, since depressive symptoms have now dominated 'most' of the total illness duration and psychotic symptoms persist beyond the mood episode (present before depression onset), this supports schizoaffective disorder, depressive type (F25.1) over major depressive disorder with psychotic features, since psychosis preceded and outlasts the mood disturbance. F20.0 is ruled out because there has been a clear, sustained mood episode (depressive) that is not brief relative to the psychotic illness.

opening_question.intent: Establish the primary reason for the visit and gather the patient's presenting concern
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports auditory hallucinations (a woman's voice calling her name), olfactory hallucinations (smell of burning metal), and persecutory delusions (belief customers were watching/surveilling the shop) that began and persisted for several weeks while mood and energy were completely normal, satisfying the requirement for psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of a mood episode for at least 2 weeks. Subsequently, a major depressive episode developed (anhedonia, fatigue, insomnia, appetite loss, guilt, cognitive/tangential speech) with psychotic symptoms continuing concurrently. Mood symptoms have been present for the majority of the total illness duration. No manic/hypomanic symptoms were reported (patient explicitly denies elevated mood, increased energy, or euphoria), and no substances, medications, or medical/neurological conditions account for the symptoms. This pattern—psychotic symptoms preceding and outlasting a mood episode, with mood symptoms present most of the time—is classic for Schizoaffective Disorder, depressive type, distinguishing it from MDD with psychotic features (where psychosis is mood-congruent and only during mood episode) and from Schizophrenia (where mood symptoms would not dominate the clinical picture).
